results.title: Plasma-Derived Mediators Flashcards | Quizlet
results.content: # Plasma-Derived Mediators. 4 properties of plasma-derived mediators? - tightly-controlled: active mediators produced only in response to stimulus such as microbes or material from necrotic cells (aka initiating mediators) -- ensures inflammation triggered only when needed! 4 properties of plasma-derived mediators? - tightly-controlled: active mediators produced only in response to stimulus such as microbes or material from necrotic cells (aka initiating mediators) -- ensures inflammation triggered only when needed! plasma derived mediators are circulating factors in the plasma. the major cell types that produce cell-derived mediators of acute inflammation are the sentinels (soldiers/guards) that detect invaders and damage in tissues, that is, macrophages, dendritic cells, and mast cells; but platelets, neutrophils, endothelial cells, and even most epithelia can be induced to elaborate some of the mediators. where are most plasma-derived mediators produced? another name for plasma-derived mediators? how are plasma-derived mediators present in the circulation? plasma consists mostly of water with various electrolytes, enzymes, clotting factors, and a number of other proteins (including plasma-derived inflammatory mediators). interrelated systems of plasma derived mediators? complement proteins are present as inactive forms (zymogens) in plasma, many become activated to make proteolytic enzymes that degrade other complement proteins, forming an enzymatic cascade capable of lots of amplification. lectin pathway -- in which plasma mannose-binding lectin (MBL) binds to carbohydrates on microbes and directly activates another complement molecule, C1. C3a is released, C3b binds microbe or cell where complement is being activated. C3b can further activate the alternative pathway in a feed forward type mechanism or it can contribute to formation of **C5 convertase** which cleaves C5 generating C5a, releasing it and C5b which attaches to microbe/cell surface, binds late complement components (C6-C9) culminating in the formation of a membrane attack complex (MAC). 1. inflammation: C3a and C5a are cleavage products that stimulate histamine (cell-derived mediator) release from mast cells, which increases vascular permeability and causes vasodilation. C5a can also activate the **lipooxygenase pathway** (more cell-derived mediators) in arachidonic acid metabolism in neutrophils and monocytes leading to further release of inflammatory mediators. Kinins are vasoactive peptides derived from plasma proteins known as kininogens by the activity of specific proteases called kallikreins. Factor XIIa from the coagulation cascade converts plasma prekallikrein into an active proteolytic form kallikrein.

results.title: Pre-Mediation and Initial Caucus Strategies for a ...
results.content: This article will address key mediator strategies prior to the mediation session and during the initial caucus to improve the chances of reaching a settlement — and satisfying the expectations of litigants and their counsel. Before mediation begins, mediators should invest time in thoroughly understanding the nature of the dispute and the parties involved. 1. **Gathering information — pre-mediation submissions.** As part of the mediation scheduling process, the mediator should tell counsel what he or she expects regarding the submission of a mediation position paper, including relevant documents, pleadings, legal agreements, and any communication between the parties to gain a comprehensive understanding of the dispute’s background and complexities. The focus should be on parties who have never participated in a mediation, often a “novice” plaintiff. Two key topics are confidentiality and the fact that the lawyer/mediator will not provide legal advice to any party. Thus, in the later situation, the burden is on the party and counsel to assert confidentiality; otherwise, the mediator can use what he or she learns to move the parties closer together. This also allows the parties to understand the mediation’s trajectory and goals. 3. **Decide on a joint session, “meet and greet,” or keep the parties apart.** Getting all parties and counsel together for a short “meet-and-greet” session allows the mediator to reiterate the ground rules and gives each attorney to opportunity to introduce themselves and their clients and say a few words if they wish. This is especially important in pre-suit mediations or cases where the parties have not yet been deposed. The mediator should learn at the initial caucus, if not before, whether the parties should not be in the same room because of the history between them. Starting with the initial caucus, mediators should work to increase the balance in their “Trust Bank” from each party. 6. **Demonstrate neutrality.** Mediators must demonstrate impartiality and neutrality throughout the process to gain the trust of both parties and encourage open communication. By investing time in understanding the parties, setting the stage for constructive dialogue, and building rapport and trust, mediators can significantly enhance the likelihood of achieving a successful resolution.

results.title: Mediation preparation and negotiating strategies
results.content: *Talk to the client about the purpose of mediation, including its benefits and negatives.* American Bar Association, Section of Litigation, Ethical Guideline for Settlement Negotiations 3.1.1 provides that “A lawyer should consider and discuss with the client, promptly after retention in a dispute … possible alternatives to conventional litigation, including settlement.” Clients should be told about the risks of litigation, mediation costs and the financial advantages and disadvantages of settling or going to trial, including remaining pre-trial motions that still must be heard and the substantial benefit of mediation confidentiality. *Discuss the case with the mediator beforehand.* A pre-mediation conference may be helpful if there is a need to advise the mediator about the non-attendance of a party (see Rule of Court 3.874) or to learn whether the mediator has particular requirements regarding briefs and exhibits. *Analyze the factual and legal strengths and weaknesses of both your case and the opposing party’s.* Be ready to discuss with the mediator the strengths and weaknesses of your case. *Exchange mediation briefs with opposing counsel.* Most attorneys do not send their briefs to opposing counsel, which means that mediators, with the consent of the parties, must spend valuable time educating both parties about known facts, laws and contentions. Discuss with the mediator which party should commence the negotiation phase. *The second stage of a mediation is the introductory phase* in which the mediator talks to the parties separately about that day’s process, including confidentiality, and that he or she will only discuss the contents of confidential briefs with opposing counsel’s consent. With the approval of all parties, the mediator proposes a settlement in writing that he or she hopes, based on the prior discussions, will be acceptable to everyone. At this point in the process, a reasoned proposal has a substantial chance of being accepted because the settlement is being suggested by the mediator, a neutral third party, and the mediator, after much discussion, should be seen by all concerned as informed, knowledgeable, fair and credible.
